title: Democrats’ midterm wave reached state legislatures. That brings pressure to deliver.
text:
Democrats’ midterm wave reached state legislatures. That brings pressure to deliver.
Democrats’ midterm success has given them a majority in more state legislatures, where the pressure to deliver results is as keen as it is nationally.
The blue wave that set up Democrats to take control of both chambers of Congress next year also handed the Democratic Party a majority of state legislatures across the country.
In 22 states, Democrats will hold the governorship as well as both houses of the state legislature. This means that in 2027, there will almost certainly be a second blue wave of bills and initiatives Democrats hope will deliver on issues such as improving affordability, protecting voter rights, and expanding access to health insurance.
In Wisconsin, Democrats will have a trifecta for the first time since Republicans swept into control in 2010. Incoming state Senate Majority Leader Dianne Hesselbein says Democrats must deliver on their campaign promises, including fully funding public schools, lowering grocery prices, and reducing high property taxes.
The midterm elections ushered in Democratic control of Congress, but also of more state legislatures across the United States. Those bodies will be tackling a wide range of issues with urgency to deliver for voters, and their decisions could play a role in national policymaking.
“We must confront the causes of that [affordability] crisis and that starts with strengthening our democracy so that our government is responsive to the people,” Senator Hesselbein writes in an email to the Monitor.
When the new year starts, nearly 53% of all Americans will live in a state where Democrats control the executive and legislative branches. Republicans will retain control of both houses of the legislature in 19 states, a drop from 28 before the election. Democrats say they know they’ve been elected to improve voters’ quality of life, and they may face the same verdict as Republicans in two years if they fail.
Variety of issues in play at state level
Pocketbook issues such as high grocery bills and fuel costs were a major driver for voters across the United States, but there were other issues. In Arizona, Democrats rode to power promising to rein in school-voucher programs and tamp down rising utility bills. In Pennsylvania, they promised to increase funding for mass transit, raise the minimum wage, increase access to housing, and protect abortion rights. In Texas, Wisconsin, and Michigan, voters supported Democratic candidates who promised to regulate data centers.
Thad Kousser, a political scientist at the University of California San Diego, says that voters send people to office for relatively short terms in state elections, and they expect results.
“So in two years' time in the legislatures, four years' time in most of these governorships, they're going to have to deliver something on the key things, the key parts of affordability and access to healthcare.”
In Pennsylvania, Democratic lawmakers are signalling they will prioritize affordability starting with bills that had gained bipartisan support but failed to pass Republican-controlled committees in the state Senate.
On the day after the election, Democratic State House Leader Matthew Bradford told supporters, “We are humbled, and we are so excited by the opportunity in front of us.” There are hundreds of bills stuck in committee, he says.
“It's everything. Like, why does private equity own our hospitals? And why is it OK that Pennsylvania pays its workers $7.25 an hour? These things are finally going to be addressed in a real way in Harrisburg.”
Chris Warshaw, a Georgetown University political science professor, says in places where power is divided, Democrats will likely focus on issues that are less partisan, such as data centers. “I expect places all over the country are going to enact various regulations and potentially bans on data centers, and I think that will be certainly true in blue states, but also in some of these purple states.” Passing more liberal bills in purple states will be “a tougher slog,” he adds.
What states do can matter nationally
This coming wave of Democratic measures addressing affordability in the states could trickle up to the national political scene, says Jaclyn Kettler, a political science professor at Boise State University. State legislatures are often test labs for new solutions to practical problems.
“State legislatures can diffuse policy ideas across states, but also up and down between the federal government and state governments,” she says. She notes that President Barack Obama studied Massachusetts’ health insurance system when constructing his Affordable Care Act.
“I think that that might be one quick way for the new Democratic majority in Congress to get rolling: what have some of the Democratic states been doing, and where have they had success in either addressing problems that Democrats are concerned about, or have proved to be popular or successful solutions?”
If Democrats push too hard for progressive initiatives, they risk losing some of the independents and conservatives who moved away from President Donald Trump’s Republican Party. But if they’re too cautious, they could lose the opportunity to make the kind of substantial changes their core supporters are expecting.
Steven Rogers, a political science professor at Saint Louis University, says that the danger of Democratic overreach is real, particularly in states and districts that have traditionally voted Republican. Arizona, for instance, will have a Democratic House, Senate, and governor’s mansion for the first time in six decades.
“I think to the extent that this was about affordability and pain, the voters were pointing the finger at Trump; they couldn't vote against him, but they whacked his party,” he says. Mr. Trump is term-limited, and without his galvanizing effect on Republicans and triggering effect on Democrats, in 2028 many voters may return to their “natural” ideological home.
“What's going to be conscious in these Democrats' minds is that they are holding a lot of seats they should not be holding. They earned the seats, they’re elected to the seats, but they’re not natural Democratic seats,” Mr. Rogers says.
The question, he says, is whether 2026 signals a major political shift, as happened after the housing crisis of 2008, or whether it will be only a temporary rebuke.
